answers_by_date.answer: Yes, all migrants can obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 346 (restored by Ley 23.059 of 1984, as amended by Leyes 24.533 and 24.951) and its regulation, Decreto 3213/84, set naturalization conditions (age 18, two years' continuous residence, a declaration before a federal judge) and nowhere require renouncing the nationality of origin. In practice the federal courts' citizenship application form contained a 'renuncia a la nacionalidad de origen' clause until the July 2010 plenary removed it. That practice is documented only in 2010 reports; there is no source from around 2000.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, all migrants can obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: The statutory position was unchanged: Decreto 1601/2004 replaced only art. 2 of Decreto 3213/84, on the option for children of native Argentines. The renunciation clause in the judicial form was still in use. Its effect on the nationality of origin depended on that country's law. No practice source specific to 2005.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, all migrants can obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: The law was unchanged. CSJN 'Padilla, Miguel' (10 April 2007) stated that one may naturalize as an Argentine without losing the nationality of origin; the ruling was not read in full here, only quoted in reports. On 1 January 2010 the form still carried the renunciation clause; the Cámara Nacional en lo Civil y Comercial Federal en pleno ordered it removed in 'Zunino, Ignacio s/ petición' on 1 July 2010.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, all migrants can obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 346 and Decreto 3213/84 still had no renunciation requirement. Ley 26.774 (2012) changed only art. 7 (voting age). The 2010 plenary had removed the renunciation clause from the form. No documented pattern of breach was found for this period.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

Ratifican en Pleno que No se Puede Renunciar a la Nacionalidad de Origen (abogados.com.ar)

answers.sourcing_note: The InfoLEG consolidated text of Ley 346 lists every amendment with its date. Together with the Decreto 3213/84 consolidated text, it shows that no renunciation requirement existed at any date between 2000 and 2020. Neither 'Padilla' nor 'Zunino' could be read in full (CSJN text not located; HCDN and Refworld PDFs timed out or were blocked), so both rulings are known only through press reports, and the renunciation-form practice is dated only by the 2010 plenary.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'Yes' holds, but it rests on the statute rather than on 'Padilla'. Padilla concerned an Argentine-born national holding Italian nationality, so its dictum on naturalization is obiter, and the ruling was not read in full. What carries the answer is that Ley 346 and Decreto 3213/84 impose no renunciation. Whether the nationality of origin is actually retained also depends on the law of the country of origin, which Argentine law cannot guarantee.
answers.notes: Implementation drops to 'Usually' for 2000–2010 because the courts' application form required a formal renunciation of the nationality of origin until the 'Zunino' plenary of 1 July 2010. That renunciation had no basis in Argentine law, and its effect depended on the law of the country of origin. The 1969 Argentina–Spain and 1971 Argentina–Italy dual-nationality agreements also applied throughout the period.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439 (Ley Videla) art. 21 gave a revocable 'residencia precaria' to foreigners 'que gestionen la regularización de su permanencia'. Under art. 37, however, the authority faced with an illegal stay could only order departure or expulsion, and art. 30 barred irregular migrants from working. Beyond that, regularization came through one-off amnesties and the 1998 Argentina–Bolivia migration agreement (amended in 2000), which opened time-limited windows for nationals in an irregular situation. IOM (2012) reports 156,000 regularizations through amnesty decrees in 1992–2003, while restrictive rules produced thousands of new irregular migrants each year.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 25.871 (B.O. 21 January 2004) had replaced Ley 22.439. Art. 17 obliges the State to adopt measures to regularize migrants, and art. 61 says the DNM 'deberá conminarlo a regularizar su situación' before ordering expulsion. Decreto 836/2004 created the Programa Nacional de Normalización Documentaria Migratoria, and Decreto 1169/2004 (B.O. 13 September 2004) regularized non-MERCOSUR nationals resident by 30 June 2004 (more than 12,000 people). Patria Grande (Disposición 53.253/2005) did not start until December 2005. IOM reports more than 400,000 regularized in 2003–2006.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 25.871 arts. 17 and 61 were in force but not yet regulated (Decreto 616/2010 came only in May 2010). The Patria Grande programme was under way. The UN Committee on Migrant Workers (2011) found that more than half of 423,711 MERCOSUR applicants received residence, but it was concerned that the DNM did not consider personal circumstances before expulsion, and it recommended wider access to regularization.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 25.871 arts. 17 and 61 were now regulated by Decreto 616/2010. Its art. 61 requires the DNM to give the irregular migrant 30 days, extendable by 30 more, to regularize, and its art. 17 allows simplified procedures and special programmes, such as Disposición 979/2014 for Korean nationals. Practice evidence for this period is thin: CELS reports on territorial outreach and its end in late 2015 were seen only in search results.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The protection answer holds. The 2020 implementation rating 'Usually; Rarely' joins two levels that are not neighbours, so it is not a valid rating on the scale. It probably reflects the gap between ordinary regularization and the narrowing under DNU 70/2017 (summary expulsions, the end of territorial outreach). The 2023 citation quotes the 2025 wording of art. 61 ('podrá intimarlo'), which did not exist in 2020; on 1 January 2020 art. 61 read 'deberá conminarlo', which is stronger.
answers.notes: For 2000 the 'Yes' is weaker: Ley 22.439 art. 21 recognized regularization requests (residencia precaria), but art. 37 provided only departure or expulsion. Actual routes were one-off amnesties and bilateral windows for Bolivian (and Peruvian) nationals. The change is coded 'not the same' because the 2004 law turned an ad hoc possibility into a statutory duty to regularize before expulsion (arts. 17 and 61), and implementation also rose.

answers_by_date.basis: Ley 346 art. 1 inc. 1 makes Argentine everyone born in the territory 'sea cual fuere la nacionalidad de sus padres'. The American Convention art. 20(2) (the right to the nationality of the state of birth if the person has no other) has constitutional rank under art. 75 inc. 22. Constitution art. 20 and Ley 346 art. 2 allow naturalization after two years' residence, and Ley 19.510 made Argentina party to the 1954 Statelessness Convention. No practice evidence specific to 2000 was found; the rating is carried over from the starting level.

Unchanged: ius soli under Ley 346 art. 1, plus the constitutional-rank American Convention art. 20(2) and general naturalization under Ley 346 art. 2 and Decreto 3213/84 art. 3. There was no statelessness-determination procedure. No practice evidence for this period.

Law unchanged. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (June 2010) welcomed free, universal birth registration but found insufficient provincial implementation, leaving many children born outside health facilities or in remote areas without registration. That gap affects access in practice to ius soli nationality.
Law unchanged: ius soli and general naturalization, with no stateless-specific procedure until Ley 27.512 (B.O. 28 August 2019). No practice source for around 2015 could be read.

answers.sourcing_note: The ius soli rule (Ley 346 art. 1) and the American Convention art. 20 are unchanged throughout and were read in the InfoLEG texts, and the Ley 27.512 dates were read in the Boletín Oficial. Practice evidence is thin: the CRC 2010 observations concern children generally rather than stateless migrants specifically, and UNHCR and Cancillería PDFs could not be opened. The law approving the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness could not be verified.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 'Yes' holds: Ley 27.512 was published on 28 August 2019 and in force by 1 January 2020. The guarantee for children rests mainly on ius soli (Ley 346 art. 1 inc. 1) and the constitutional-rank American Convention art. 20(2). For stateless adult migrants the law gives a right to naturalize rather than an automatic grant, and on 1 January 2020 DNU 70/2017 still required two years of legal residence.
answers.notes: The 'Yes' for 2000–2015 rests on unconditional ius soli and the constitutional-rank American Convention art. 20(2), both in force throughout. Ley 27.512 (2019) added a stateless-specific naturalization right, so the protection changed in content although the answer did not. Implementation is kept at the starting level 'Sometimes; Usually' for lack of contrary evidence; the only practice source read (CRC 2010) documents gaps in birth registration.
